Germany suspended the gold standard at the onset of WW1, in order to give them the financial flexibility they needed to fund the war. When Germany exited the war the papiermark was relatively stable (albeit endangered by massive sovereign debt), but it dived off a cliff when the allies insisted the Germans begin paying their war debt in gold or foreign currency. The only way Germany could do this was by mass printing of marks (something which would be impossible on the gold standard) to buy gold and foreign currency to satisfy the allies' demands. This of course tanked the value of the mark, which plunged Germany into serious economic depression.

To make matters worse, when they tried to temporarily suspend reparations to rescue their economy, the French and Belgians invaded the Ruhr and demanded they be paid in coal instead. The German government directed the miners to strike and funded the strike with yet more papiermarks, further reducing their value.

After that they managed to eventually stabilise the mark by creating a new currency called the "rentenmark" (mortgage-mark) which was based on the industrial wealth of the country and (as far as I can tell) financed through wealth taxes.
